rv.q: Mantell’s approach is more straightforward, more eager to move us, and ultimately less moving.

Mantell and Battat are able to inject the piece with some hope: hope in the power of collective action, hope that the individual bonds between people might yet be saved.
The playwright hasn’t worked out the internal logic of such a world: Much is vague; what few details exist can’t withstand much scrutiny.
I wanted to be shocked and galvanized by the collision of corporate cruelty and human kindness, but Parking Lot peters out in its climactic scenes.

If Mantell’s mournful In the Amazon Warehouse Parking Lot is scarcely a crowd-pleaser, it is a sensitively crafted drama commissioned and produced by Playwrights Horizons, where its world premiere opened Monday.
A tantalizingly dark premise, it proves to be merely drab under the slack direction of Sivan Battat, dulled further by listless performances.
The creative team successfully evokes director Sivan Battat’s vision for Mantell’s play.
Just like Amazon, in the end, Mantell’s gripping play delivers.

cn.t: Mantell's dystopian drama about queer women surviving as Amazon warehouse workers earns mixed reviews for its timely themes of climate catastrophe and capitalism, though critics find the execution underdeveloped despite strong camaraderie among characters.
